question: A 72-year-old T2DM patient presents with confusion and lethargy over 3 days. Blood glucose is 720 mg/dL, serum osmolality 345 mOsm/kg, pH 7.38, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, urine ketones trace. Which diagnosis and immediate priority best describes this presentation?

answers.text: Severe DKA — start insulin infusion and IV normal saline immediately

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: DKA requires significant acidosis (pH <7.30, bicarb <15) and ketonaemia — neither is present here. pH 7.38 and bicarb 22 are normal. This is not DKA.

answers.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) — priority is gradual rehydration with careful monitoring

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Glucose >600 mg/dL + serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg + absent acidosis + minimal ketones = HHS. The key management principle is gradual rehydration (to correct fluid deficit over 24-48h), because rapid rehydration risks cerebral oedema. Insulin is added only after adequate fluid replacement is underway.

answers.text: Euglycaemic DKA — the normal pH may be falsely reassuring

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Euglycaemic DKA has normal or near-normal glucose (typically <250 mg/dL) but significant acidosis and ketonaemia. This patient has extreme hyperglycaemia with no acidosis — the opposite pattern.
Lactic acidosis presents with metabolic acidosis (low pH, low bicarbonate, elevated anion gap). pH 7.38 and bicarb 22 are normal, making lactic acidosis very unlikely.

overallFeedback.feedback: HHS vs DKA: In HHS, glucose is typically >600 mg/dL, osmolality >320 mOsm/kg, pH is normal (>7.30), and ketones are absent/trace. DKA has lower glucose (250-500), pH <7.30, significant ketonaemia. Management differs: HHS = rehydration first; DKA = fluids + insulin + electrolyte correction simultaneously.
Correct — HHS = extreme hyperglycaemia (>600) + hyperosmolality (>320) + no significant acidosis + minimal ketones. Gradual rehydration is the priority.
